paragraphs: Machine learning methods for mixed-integer linear programs need representative problem instances for training and evaluation. When real examples are scarce, learned decisions can suffer and solver assessments can become biased. This paper introduces G2MILP, a deep generative framework intended to produce additional instances that retain important characteristics of real problems without requiring expert-designed formulations.

G2MILP represents each optimization instance as a bipartite graph and uses a masked variational autoencoder to modify it. The generation process repeatedly corrupts and replaces portions of an existing graph. This gives the model a way to learn patterns from available instances and use those patterns to construct new problems, rather than relying entirely on manually specified generation rules.

The authors develop benchmarks that assess both structural resemblance and computational difficulty. Their experiments show that generated instances can closely match real datasets along both dimensions. Preserving difficulty matters because superficially similar problems need not challenge a solver similarly. The findings support using generated instances to help downstream solver development when real-world data is limited.
neurips-2023-a-deep-instance-generative-.tldr: G2MILP generates new optimization instances that empirically resemble real datasets in structure and computational difficulty.

paragraphs: Molecular graph neural networks have become more accurate as their architectures have grown more complex, but that complexity makes large-scale applications expensive. This paper investigates whether knowledge distillation can transfer useful information from larger teacher models to smaller student models. The goal is to improve the students’ predictions while retaining the inference speed of their existing architectures.

The authors develop strategies for transferring hidden representations in directional and equivariant graph neural networks. They evaluate these strategies on energy and force prediction, testing different teacher–student combinations and datasets. They also optimize components of the distillation framework and investigate whether data augmentation can further improve performance. The approach changes how students learn without modifying their architectures.

Across the evaluated configurations, distillation consistently improves student accuracy. The reported improvements close as much as 96.7% of the teacher–student accuracy gap for energy prediction and 62.5% for force prediction, while preserving student inference throughput. These percentages describe reductions in an accuracy gap, not absolute accuracy scores. The results show that lightweight molecular models can gain substantially from richer models during training.
neurips-2023-accelerating-molecular-grap.tldr: Distilling hidden representations improves lightweight molecular models’ energy and force predictions while preserving their inference throughput.

paragraphs: Adaptive data analysis asks a mechanism to answer statistical questions using samples from an unknown distribution, with later questions depending on earlier answers. Previous computational hardness results relied on an adversarial analyst who also selected the distribution. That analyst therefore had an informational advantage over the mechanism, raising questions about how well the setting represents an analyst seeking unknown information.

This paper studies balanced adversaries by separating two roles. A sampler chooses the distribution and supplies samples, while an analyst selects adaptive queries without prior knowledge of that distribution. Under standard public-key cryptography assumptions, the authors revisit earlier lower bounds using an efficient adversary that respects this separation. Thus, computational difficulty persists in a setting with a more balanced allocation of knowledge.

The paper also examines why stronger cryptographic assumptions appear in this construction. It shows that any computationally bounded balanced adversary with the structure shared by known attacks would imply public-key cryptography. This conclusion concerns that attack structure; it does not establish that every conceivable balanced attack requires it. The contribution clarifies both the hardness result and the assumptions supporting it.
neurips-2023-adaptive-data-analysis-in-a.tldr: Adaptive-query hardness persists with a less informed analyst under public-key cryptographic assumptions, whose necessity is established for known attack structures.

paragraphs: A probabilistic forecast is calibrated when its stated probabilities agree with observed frequencies. Calibration is valuable only alongside useful predictions: adjusting probabilities after training can make forecasts less sharp, or less informative about particular outcomes. This paper approaches calibration as a distribution-matching problem, aiming to make it part of model training rather than relying solely on later corrections.

The authors introduce kernel-based metrics that bring together and extend familiar calibration notions for classification and regression. Their sample-based estimates are differentiable, so a model can optimize a calibration objective alongside its usual training loss. The framework also provides ways to tailor calibration to a decision task, connecting it to accurate loss estimation and decisions satisfying a no-regret criterion.

In the reported experiments, using these metrics as regularizers improves calibration, forecast sharpness, and decision-making across classification and regression tasks. The approach outperforms methods that depend only on post-training recalibration. These findings support treating uncertainty quality as a training objective, with the metric chosen to reflect how predictions will inform decisions.
neurips-2023-calibration-by-distribution.tldr: Differentiable calibration metrics let models learn better uncertainty estimates during training and improve decision-making in the reported evaluations.

paragraphs: Pseudo-labeling uses a model’s predictions as training labels for otherwise unlabeled examples. In multi-label learning, an example may belong to several classes, and the number of applicable labels is unknown. Conventional pseudo-labeling can therefore assign labels that should be absent or overlook labels that should be present. This paper proposes Class-Aware Pseudo-Labeling, or CAP, to address those errors.

CAP places class-specific thresholds inside a regularized learning framework to control positive and negative pseudo-label assignments. Its central idea is to use estimated class frequencies to guide those thresholds, aligning the distribution of pseudo-labels with the true class distribution. The authors observe that even a small labeled portion can provide a reliable approximation of class frequencies.

The paper supplies theoretical support for the distribution estimate and a generalization error bound for CAP. Experiments on multiple benchmark datasets also support the method’s effectiveness. Together, these results suggest that class prevalence is useful information when selecting pseudo-labels: prediction confidence can be interpreted alongside how frequently a class is expected to occur.
neurips-2023-class-distribution-aware-ps.tldr: CAP uses estimated class frequencies to set class-specific pseudo-label thresholds for learning from partially labeled multi-label data.

paragraphs: Federated learning can exclude resource-constrained devices when the shared model is too large for them to train. One response is to extract smaller models for different clients, allowing more devices to participate. Although this strategy has worked empirically, its convergence has lacked a general theoretical account. This paper develops a unified framework for algorithms that extract such reduced models during training.

The analysis establishes sufficient conditions under which these heterogeneous algorithms converge to a stationary point of the standard federated learning objective. It covers both identically distributed and non-identically distributed client data, for general smooth cost functions. A stationary point is the stated target of the guarantee; the result does not claim convergence to a globally optimal solution.

The authors introduce a minimum coverage index and consider it alongside noise caused by model reduction. Their analysis identifies both as factors governing convergence. The practical implication is that choosing smaller client models requires attention to more than local computational savings. How model extraction covers parameters and how much reduction disturbs learning must be considered together.
neurips-2023-every-parameter-matters-ens.tldr: A unified analysis gives sufficient conditions for federated learning with dynamically reduced client models to converge to a stationary point.

paragraphs: This paper studies intermittent reasoning failures in Transformers through a deliberately simple language-modeling task. The authors call the failures attention glitches: situations in which the architecture’s built-in tendencies do not support robust reasoning. Their objective is to isolate a possible source of brittleness without requiring the full complexity of natural language, factual knowledge, and extended reasoning to be analyzed together.

They introduce flip-flop language modeling, a configurable family of synthetic benchmarks. A model must copy binary symbols across long gaps while ignoring intervening tokens. This setup probes extrapolation and long-range dependencies with a clear target behavior. Transformer models exhibit a long tail of sporadic errors even in this simplified setting, and regularization techniques eliminate some of those errors.

Preliminary mechanistic analyses suggest that the remaining failures may be difficult to diagnose and repair. The authors hypothesize that attention glitches could explain some closed-domain hallucinations in natural language models. That connection remains a hypothesis: the demonstrated finding is intermittent failure on the synthetic task, providing a focused setting in which to investigate robustness.
neurips-2023-exposing-attention-glitches.tldr: A simple long-range copying benchmark exposes sporadic Transformer errors that regularization only partly resolves.

paragraphs: Generating samples with a diffusion model involves solving a reverse stochastic differential equation or a corresponding ordinary differential equation. Stochastic solvers can produce higher-quality samples and suit image translation, but face a trade-off between speed and effectiveness. This paper investigates a potential cause: with few discretization steps, the distribution describing a reverse transition may not be well represented by a single Gaussian.

The proposed Gaussian Mixture Solvers replace that single-Gaussian transition assumption with a mixture of Gaussians. At each sampling step, the solver estimates moments through third order and fits the mixture’s parameters using a generalized method of moments. This provides a richer transition model while retaining the stochastic sampling formulation used by SDE-based solvers.

Experiments evaluate image generation and stroke-guided synthesis across several diffusion models. The proposed solver produces better sample quality than numerous other SDE-based solvers in those evaluations. These results support the authors’ explanation that transition-distribution mismatch contributes to the efficiency–quality problem. They also show the value of improving the sampling procedure through a more expressive transition approximation.
neurips-2023-gaussian-mixture-solvers-fo.tldr: Gaussian Mixture Solvers improve diffusion sample quality by fitting richer reverse-transition distributions at each stochastic sampling step.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning can treat decision-making as supervised learning from previously collected trajectories. Sequence models are often used to process those trajectories, but their specific contribution is not always clear. This paper asks whether they compress experience into representations that are useful for learning policies, separating the representation-learning question from the subsequent task of choosing actions.

The authors use a two-stage framework. First, a sequence model encodes trajectory-level representations. Second, a goal-conditioned policy learns with those representations as inputs. Several existing supervised approaches to offline reinforcement learning fit within this formulation. The paper introduces Goal-Conditioned Predictive Coding, or GCPC, as an objective for learning representations that encode future trajectories in relation to a goal.

Evaluations on AntMaze, FrankaKitchen, and Locomotion show that sequence modeling can substantially affect performance on challenging decision-making tasks. GCPC achieves competitive performance on all three benchmarks. The findings support the usefulness of goal-related future information in a learned representation, while the two-stage organization helps identify how sequence modeling contributes to policy learning.
neurips-2023-goal-conditioned-predictive.tldr: GCPC learns goal-conditioned representations of future trajectories that support competitive offline reinforcement learning across three benchmarks.

paragraphs: An agent learning among other agents faces an environment shaped by others’ goals and adaptive behavior. This paper studies how an agent can influence those behaviors by providing information. The idea comes from information design in economics: a sender communicates information to affect a receiver’s actions, rather than influencing the receiver through tangible rewards or goods.

Applying this idea to reinforcement learning creates two challenges. Signals immediately change how trajectories unfold, adding another source of non-stationarity. Receivers can also ignore the information, so a useful signaling strategy must account for their willingness to follow it. The authors formulate a Markov signaling game and introduce a signaling gradient together with extended obedience constraints to address these issues.

The resulting algorithm is reported to be efficient on several tasks involving mixed motives. These tasks make the distinction between sending information and inducing a response especially relevant, because agents have their own objectives. The work connects adaptive signaling to reinforcement learning while explicitly accounting for the receiver’s incentives, and provides further insight into information design in computational economics.
neurips-2023-information-design-in-multi.tldr: A Markov signaling framework lets reinforcement learning agents influence others through information while accounting for changing trajectories and receiver incentives.

paragraphs: Training graph neural networks on large graphs often requires sampling a manageable portion of the graph for each mini-batch. However, expanding sampled neighborhoods can still pull in too many vertices, while other sampling approaches can compromise performance. This paper introduces LAyer-neighBOR sampling, or LABOR, to reduce the number of sampled vertices without sacrificing the reported learning quality.

LABOR is designed to replace ordinary Neighbor Sampling directly while using the same fanout hyperparameter. Its construction matches the estimator variance of Neighbor Sampling when considered from the perspective of an individual vertex. This makes the comparison more informative than a reduction in sampled vertices alone: the method preserves a stated local statistical property while changing overall sampling requirements.

The authors report sampling up to seven times fewer vertices without losing quality. With equal vertex-sampling budgets, LABOR converges faster than existing layer-sampling approaches and can accommodate batch sizes up to 112 times larger than Neighbor Sampling. These are reported upper-end gains. The results show how sampling design can substantially change the scale of graph training.
neurips-2023-layer-neighbor-sampling-def.tldr: LABOR reduces sampled graph vertices while matching Neighbor Sampling’s per-vertex estimator variance and supporting larger training batches.

paragraphs: Algorithms for efficient language-model training promise better results within a given amount of computation. This paper reexamines three families of such methods: changing the architecture during training, selecting which batches receive computation, and using alternative optimizers. The investigation asks whether their reported advantages remain when the comparison uses a fixed computational budget and a baseline whose learning rate has fully decayed.

The authors study BERT and T5 pretraining, including layer stacking and dropping, selective backpropagation and RHO-loss, and the Lion and Sophia optimizers. In these evaluations, the methods’ advantages in training, validation, and downstream performance disappear relative to that baseline. The finding emphasizes that the baseline’s learning-rate schedule is consequential when judging training efficiency.

The paper also proposes reference system time, an evaluation protocol that maps computation performed on different machines to a common reference machine. This is intended to enable comparisons across hardware, and the authors discuss the protocol’s limitations. The results challenge the tested efficiency gains under the stated setup, without establishing that these methods cannot help in other training settings.
neurips-2023-no-train-no-gain-revisiting.tldr: In fixed-budget BERT and T5 experiments, several efficient-training methods lose their advantage against a baseline with a fully decayed learning rate.

paragraphs: Learning a planning heuristic from solved problems requires deciding what the heuristic should be trained to predict. A natural target is the remaining cost of reaching the goal. This paper argues that accurately estimating that quantity can be unnecessarily difficult when the practical objective is to guide a search algorithm toward the states it should explore.

The authors revisit necessary and sufficient conditions for strictly optimally efficient heuristics, focusing mainly on A* and greedy best-first search. Here, strict optimal efficiency means expanding only states on the optimal path that the search ultimately returns. Using these conditions, they propose a family of ranking losses tailored to the particular forward-search variant, tying the learning objective to the ordering needed by that algorithm.

From a learning-theory perspective, the paper explains why estimating exact cost-to-go can demand more than search guidance requires. Experiments on a diverse set of problems strongly support the derived theory. The central contribution is an alignment between the training objective and search behavior: learning useful rankings can target the decisions the planner actually makes.
neurips-2023-optimize-planning-heuristic.tldr: Search-specific ranking losses train planning heuristics around the ordering needed for efficient search, avoiding unnecessarily difficult cost-to-go estimation.

paragraphs: The Strong Lottery Ticket Hypothesis proposes that a randomly initialized neural network is likely to contain useful subnetworks that require no weight training. Much of the existing analysis concerns unstructured pruning. Structured pruning is particularly interesting because it can offer computational and memory savings, but its mathematical analysis has been constrained by tools that do not handle the relevant dependencies.

This paper develops a suitable variant of a multidimensional random subset-sum result. The key extension accommodates stochastic dependencies that arise when analyzing structured pruning. The authors apply this mathematical tool to a broad class of random convolutional neural networks, proving that they contain structured subnetworks capable of approximating any sufficiently smaller target network.

The result establishes a sub-exponential bound for the structured version of the hypothesis, with polynomial over-parameterization highlighted in the paper’s title. Its significance is an existence guarantee about what random networks can contain. The claim concerns approximation of sufficiently smaller networks, preserving the size relationship central to the theorem. It strengthens the theoretical account of how over-parameterization can support useful structured subnetworks.
neurips-2023-polynomially-over-parameter.tldr: The paper proves that a broad class of over-parameterized random convolutional networks contains structured subnetworks approximating sufficiently smaller networks.

paragraphs: Heavy-tailed rewards can produce frequent statistical outliers and stochastic learning updates with infinite second moments. Such behavior can undermine reinforcement learning methods used for evaluating or improving policies. This paper shows how dynamic gradient clipping can make temporal-difference learning robust to these rewards, and extends the approach to a natural actor-critic method built on robust temporal-difference learning.

The analysis uses linear function approximation and assumes rewards have a finite moment of order 1+p, for p between zero and one inclusive of one. Clipping controls extreme updates while introducing bias, and the authors establish a favorable balance between that bias and variability. For target error ε, robust temporal-difference learning has sample complexity O(ε^(-1/p)) with a full-rank feature matrix and O(ε^(-1-1/p)) without that assumption.

These bounds hold both in expectation and with high probability. The robust natural actor-critic variant has a sample-complexity bound of Õ(ε^(-4-2/p)), with logarithmic factors suppressed. Numerical experiments support the theoretical results. The guarantees explicitly depend on reward moments and feature assumptions, showing how statistical tail behavior affects the amount of data needed for reliable learning.
neurips-2023-provably-robust-temporal-di.tldr: Dynamic gradient clipping gives temporal-difference and natural actor-critic methods provable robustness to heavy-tailed rewards under stated moment and approximation assumptions.

paragraphs: Gradient calculations in quantum optimization become more demanding as the number of parameters increases. This paper addresses that burden by connecting natural gradient methods with Koopman operator theory, which offers linear representations of nonlinear dynamical systems. The aim is to exploit structure in the evolution of optimization updates so that gradient-based quantum optimization can progress more efficiently.

The proposed framework, Quantum-circuit Alternating Controlled Koopman learning, is abbreviated QuACK. It uses an alternating algorithm to predict gradient dynamics efficiently. Viewing optimization as an evolving dynamical process makes Koopman learning relevant: a learned representation of that process can help anticipate its behavior. The framework brings this perspective to quantum optimization and quantum machine learning applications.

Empirical studies cover quantum chemistry, condensed matter, machine learning, and noisy environments. The authors report speedups exceeding 200 times in the overparameterized regime, 10 times in the smooth regime, and 3 times in the non-smooth regime. These are regime-specific empirical results. They show substantial acceleration across the studied settings while retaining gradient-based optimization as the underlying approach.
neurips-2023-quack-accelerating-gradient.tldr: QuACK uses Koopman learning to predict quantum optimization dynamics, achieving substantial empirical speedups across several optimization regimes.

paragraphs: Masked graph modeling learns molecular representations by hiding parts of a graph and reconstructing information about the original. This paper examines two components that have received less attention than masking and encoding: the tokenizer that defines reconstruction targets and the decoder that predicts them. These choices matter because they determine what information the encoder is encouraged to preserve.

The authors compare tokenizers operating at node, edge, motif, and graph-neural-network levels, and investigate the role of decoder expressiveness. Their results show that subgraph-level targets and a sufficiently expressive decoder using remask decoding have a large effect on learned representations. The study therefore treats reconstruction targets and reconstruction machinery as central parts of the representation-learning problem.

Building on these findings, the authors introduce SimSGT, which combines a simple GNN-based tokenizer with an effective decoding strategy. Empirical evaluations show that it outperforms existing molecular self-supervised learning methods in the studied comparisons. The contribution is both a method and an explanation of why tokenizer and decoder design deserve attention when improving molecular encoders.
neurips-2023-rethinking-tokenizer-and-de.tldr: SimSGT improves molecular representation learning through subgraph-oriented tokenization and an expressive decoding strategy informed by a study of masked graph modeling.

paragraphs: Feedforward models can reconstruct implicit shapes from unoriented point clouds quickly, but their learned expectations do not always fit a new input. They may underfit the observed points or misrepresent shapes outside the training distribution, including unfamiliar topologies. This paper proposes an efficient test-time mechanism intended to remedy some of these generalization problems by adapting reconstruction to the current shape.

The method combines two sources of guidance. The neural network contributes knowledge learned across shapes, while Nyström kernel ridge regression provides regularization within the individual shape being reconstructed. Its hyperparameters are fitted to that shape. The resulting function belongs to a shape-specific reproducing kernel Hilbert space, allowing its behavior to adapt to the particular input.

This combination supplies stability and efficiency properties along with an adjustable balance between expressiveness and robustness. Experiments on synthetic and real data demonstrate improvements over baselines and state-of-the-art methods in the reported comparisons. The contribution is a way to supplement a general learned prior with shape-specific adaptation at inference time, addressing some failures of generalization.
neurips-2023-robustifying-generalizable-.tldr: Shape-specific kernel regression improves implicit reconstruction by combining a network’s learned prior with tunable test-time regularization.

paragraphs: Segment Anything in 3D, or SA3D, extends a two-dimensional segmentation model to three-dimensional objects using a neural radiance field. The NeRF connects images from different viewpoints to a shared 3D space. This lets the method use existing 2D segmentation capabilities without repeating the costly collection and annotation process for a dedicated 3D model.

A user provides a segmentation prompt, such as rough points, in one view. SAM produces a mask, which SA3D projects into a voxel-based 3D mask using the NeRF’s learned density. The method then renders the evolving mask from another viewpoint and automatically extracts reliable prompts for SAM. Alternating these projection and prompting steps progressively completes the target object’s 3D mask.

Experiments show adaptation to various scenes and segmentation within minutes. The broader contribution is a method for carrying a promptable 2D model’s outputs across views into a shared 3D representation. Its stated applicability depends on the 2D model consistently handling prompted segmentation across multiple views, making cross-view reliability a concrete condition of the approach.
neurips-2023-segment-anything-in-3d-with.tldr: SA3D combines SAM with a NeRF to grow a 3D object mask from a manual prompt in a single image.

paragraphs: A backdoored model can behave normally on benign inputs while sending inputs containing an attacker’s trigger to a chosen class. This paper studies how to purify such a model using a small clean dataset. Its starting point is a theoretical connection between backdoor risk and adversarial risk, intended to identify which adversarial failures are most relevant to purification.

The authors derive an upper bound on backdoor risk that mainly captures risk on adversarial examples shared by the original backdoored model and the purified model. This leads to a bi-level optimization problem and the Shared Adversarial Unlearning method. SAU generates these shared examples, then updates the purified model so that it classifies them correctly, disagrees with the original model, or both.

The purpose of this update is to weaken the shared adversarial behavior associated with the backdoor effect. Experiments across benchmark datasets and network architectures report state-of-the-art backdoor-defense performance. The result links a risk-bound argument to a practical purification procedure, using shared vulnerabilities between the two models to guide which behaviors should be unlearned.
neurips-2023-shared-adversarial-unlearni.tldr: SAU mitigates backdoors by generating and unlearning adversarial examples shared between a compromised model and its purified version.

paragraphs: In value-based deep reinforcement learning with a replay memory, each learning update uses a batch of previously stored transitions. Batch size specifies how many transitions are sampled for that update. Although this choice directly shapes the learning process, it is often left unchanged when researchers introduce a new algorithm. This paper treats that familiar setting as an important experimental variable.

The authors conduct a broad empirical study of batch size and find evidence that reducing it can produce substantial performance gains. This is surprising in light of the wider tendency to favor larger batches when training neural networks. The finding suggests that expectations drawn from neural-network training more generally do not automatically settle the best batch-size choice in replay-based reinforcement learning.

Additional empirical analyses investigate the observed phenomenon. The contribution is therefore an evaluation of a commonly fixed training choice, accompanied by analysis aimed at understanding its effects. The evidence supports reconsidering smaller batches in the studied setting; it does not establish that decreasing batch size always improves every reinforcement learning algorithm.
neurips-2023-small-batch-deep-reinforcem.tldr: A broad empirical study finds that smaller replay batches can substantially improve value-based deep reinforcement learning.

paragraphs: This paper investigates how one recurrent neural network develops dynamics for several tasks. The authors construct a framework that reduces interference from correlations between inputs, outputs, and hidden representations. Within that setting, they observe a tendency to share attractors and reuse existing dynamics, which they call a simplicity bias. Attractors provide shared destinations for the network’s evolving internal states.

During training, attractors emerge sequentially, and the networks preferentially reuse dynamics when possible. Concrete examples show that new attractors arise primarily in response to task demands or architectural constraints. The authors also construct task families from functions to study representation geometry inside a shared attractor. They find that function steepness controls alignment, with similarly spaced inputs undergoing comparable transformations.

These results describe a balance between reuse and pressures that demand new dynamics. The authors suggest that shared-attractor geometry might help reveal the nature of unknown tasks. They also argue that modular organization may not emerge spontaneously without specific incentives. Both implications concern what the observed simplicity bias could mean for interpreting and encouraging specialization in recurrent networks.
neurips-2023-the-simplicity-bias-in-mult.tldr: Multi-task RNNs tend to reuse dynamics and share attractors, with new attractors emerging mainly under task or architectural pressures.

paragraphs: Removal-based explanation methods assess feature contributions by considering what happens when particular features are omitted. Prominent approaches such as SHAP and LIME use this general strategy. This paper examines inconsistencies that can arise when explanation methods prioritize efficiency in their original context, asking whether those problems reflect shortcomings of particular methods or an underlying conflict among desired properties.

The authors establish an Impossible Trinity Theorem: interpretability, efficiency, and consistency cannot all hold simultaneously in the setting they analyze. This makes the conflict structural within that setting. To assess imperfect explanations, they propose interpretation error, a metric intended to capture inefficiencies and inconsistencies, and introduce two algorithms based on the standard polynomial basis that seek to minimize it.

Empirical results show substantial reductions in interpretation error, reaching up to 31.8 times lower error than alternative techniques. This finding concerns the proposed error measure and the evaluated comparisons. The work therefore combines a theoretical trade-off with an optimization target, offering a way to assess and improve explanations even when all three desired properties cannot coexist.
neurips-2023-trade-off-between-efficienc.tldr: The paper proves a three-way trade-off for removal-based explanations and proposes algorithms that substantially reduce measured interpretation error.

paragraphs: Large, over-parameterized models are costly to train, but their internal modules do not necessarily learn equally well. This paper examines learning at the level of components such as attention heads. The authors find different learning patterns across modules and introduce a modular neural tangent kernel, or mNTK, to characterize a module’s capacity to learn.

They associate learning quality with the largest eigenvalue of the module’s mNTK. Large values indicate feature learning with better convergence, while very small values may negatively affect generalization. Based on this relationship, Modular Adaptive Training selectively updates modules whose largest eigenvalue exceeds a changing threshold. The strategy aims to emphasize common features while ignoring inconsistent ones.

Selective updating reduces the need to run a complete backpropagation cycle across every module. In the reported experiments, MAT nearly halves training computation and achieves higher accuracy than the baselines. These results support allocating updates according to measured differences in module learning behavior. The reported computational and accuracy gains are empirical findings, while the kernel measure supplies the rationale for choosing which modules to update.
neurips-2023-train-faster-perform-better.tldr: MAT selectively updates modules using a kernel-based learning measure, nearly halving training computation and improving accuracy in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Document understanding requires connecting text, tables, and visual elements on a page. Models can struggle with unfamiliar domains and languages when training data lacks sufficient variety. WordScape addresses this data problem through a pipeline for creating large, multilingual collections of document images, text, and layout annotations from Word files available on the web.

The pipeline parses the files’ Open XML structure to obtain textual representations and annotated document images together. It draws on the widespread availability of Word documents through Common Crawl and can be adapted to domain-specific material. Using the structure already present in these files provides a route to naturally organized, linguistically and culturally varied pages without manually labeling every document.

The authors describe a planned release of 9.5 million document URLs that can be processed into more than 40 million pages. They also evaluate extracted text and layout annotations, assess effects on document-understanding benchmarks, and demonstrate substantial reductions in manual labeling costs. The contribution is both a scalable extraction method and evidence that its automatically produced annotations can reduce annotation effort.
neurips-2023-wordscape-a-pipeline-to-ext.tldr: WordScape turns web-hosted Word documents into multilingual text and layout-annotated page datasets, substantially reducing manual labeling costs.
